title: POC SLO sampling playbook — EmberTech kickoff
summary: Kickoff to define POC success criteria for latency/throughput SLOs. Covered TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs, concrete p95/p99 targets for EmberTech workloads, sampling/benchmark plan (warm vs cold cache, sequence-length buckets), and a 6-week pilot timeline with a stress sweep lab run. Action items assigned for benchmark spreadsheet, security checklist, and lab schedule.

p95/p99 target setting by traffic slice
workload sizing: request distribution and sequence length buckets
benchmark measurement plan: sample sizes, warm/cold, burstiness

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-27 15:30 PDT
Duration: 75 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Ava (Redwood SE), Rajesh (EmberTech Eng Lead), Maya (EmberTech SRE), Tom (EmberTech CFO), Priya (EmberTech PM)

--- Auto-summary (optional):
Quick discussion to align on SLO definitions (TTFT vs TPOT), establish p95/p99 targets by traffic slice, agree sampling plan and lab sweep cadence, and set next steps for the 6-week pilot.

00:00 Lena: All right uh good afternoon everyone thanks for joining. quick roll call?
00:14 Rajesh: Rajesh here, Maya here, Priya here. Tom will jump in for budget discussion later.
00:22 Lena: Perfect, thanks. The objective today is to lock down success criteria for the POC specifically around latency and throughput SLOs and the measurement approach. We're proposing a 6 week pilot, but we'll get into that.
00:41 Samir: I'll focus on the measurement details — sampling, warm vs cold KV cache, sequence length buckets and the actual stress sweep plan.
00:50 Priya: Our primary constraint is user-facing latency for chat — we need to make sure we capture tail behaviour during peak.
01:05 Maya: To add, on infra side we have bursty traffic — Friday afternoons spike and some background batch jobs. We'll share traces.
01:20 Lena: Great. Quick sanity check on terminology — we use TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (total per-token time, ms per token). Sometimes in docs TTFT is written T-T-F-T which confuses folks. Any preferred metric?
01:36 Rajesh: TTFT is the user-facing one, TPOT is more about cost modelling. We need both.
01:45 Samir: Agreed. For the POC we recommend acceptance criteria across both: TTFT p95/p99 and TPOT p95 for steady-state generation. Also measure cold-start p99 for first request after cache flush.
02:05 Lena: EmberTech's initial ask was p95 below 200ms for chat first token, is that right?
02:12 Rajesh: That's what leadership mentioned. But it's flexible if we can show cost tradeoffs.
02:20 Samir: From Redwood's experience, with our Dedicated pools we can often hit TTFT p95 ~120-180ms on the 70B-style models with warmed KV cache and batching tuned. TPOT depends heavily on sequence length distribution — expect 10–30ms per token in many cases, but burstiness and batch inefficiency can push that up.
03:01 Priya: So how do we pick p99 targets? Leadership cares about 99th more than 95th sometimes.
03:10 Samir: We propose two acceptance tiers:
 - Tier A (strict): TTFT p95 < 150ms, TTFT p99 < 350ms, TPOT p95 < 25ms/token
 - Tier B (lenient): TTFT p95 < 220ms, TTFT p99 < 500ms, TPOT p95 < 40ms/token
03:40 Rajesh: That seems reasonable, but we need to map those to EmberTech traffic slices — short replies vs long-form.
03:50 Lena: Right. Let's break traffic into three buckets: short (<= 32 tokens), medium (33–128), long (>128). We'll set different TPOT targets per bucket and measure TTFT mostly on short and medium where user perception matters.
04:12 Ava: Also important: cache hit rate. If prefix cache hits are low we should expect TTFT regressions. Measurement should record prefix cache hit ratio and KV cache warmness.
04:30 Maya: Our cache ephemeral duration is 30 minutes currently for some flows — we'll evaluate bumping that for the pilot.
04:38 Samir: For the benchmark we'll run both warm and cold sweeps: warm = after steady traffic for 30m, cold = after cache flush + cold-start spikes. We'll capture p95/p99 for both modes.
05:01 Lena: Good. On sampling size — what do you need from EmberTech to make p99 meaningful?
05:10 Samir: To estimate p99 with reasonable confidence we'll want at least ~5k samples per slice. For p99 is more fragile, so prefer 10k if possible across the test window. For bursty windows we should sample across multiple peaks.
05:28 Rajesh: We can pull 2 weeks of traces and extract histograms. We'll anonymize sensitive fields.
05:36 Lena: Please include peak hour traces and a mid-week low-traffic day.
05:41 Priya: We'll do that.
05:46 Samir: Measurement plan will include: request-level timings, token counts, cache-hit flag, batching size, instance type, and error codes. We'll post a template CSV.
06:05 Ava: We'll also capture system-level metrics: GPU utilization, memory, kernel stalls. That helps correlate tail latencies.
06:15 Maya: For legal reasons our team will need all data retention and PII controls documented. We flagged SOC2 and KMS earlier.
06:24 Lena: We'll attach Redwood's SOC2 snapshot and KMS options. Note that for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS.
06:35 Tom: Quick budget interjection — how much extra for dedicated reserved capacity for the 6-week pilot?
06:42 Lena: We have a pilot package with blended pricing; I'll send a cost estimate after we confirm expected tokens/peak qps.
06:53 Tom: Ok please include that in the SOW.
07:00 Rajesh: Back to sampling — what about synthetic traffic generation? We don't want production load.
07:08 Samir: We'll run a synthetic generator that replays the sequence length distribution and inter-arrival times. We can emulate burstiness via Poisson processes or shaped bursts. We'll provide the generator and the workload file.
07:24 Rajesh: For correctness we also need a set of golden prompts to ensure model quality isn't regressing under load.
07:31 Ava: Agreed — include a small evaluation set (100 prompts) and automated pass/fail thresholds for content regression. That will be outside pure latency but part of acceptance.
07:46 Priya: How do we measure TPOT as responses vary in length?
07:51 Samir: TPOT we normalize as ms/token across the response; we'll report median token time and p95 token time for each bucket. Also report per-request tokens and total response time to catch pathological cases.
08:12 Rajesh: What about the sampling cadence? Continuously during a 15 minute peak window?
08:18 Samir: We recommend run sweeps: 15-minute peak windows sampled at 1s resolution aggregated, plus full 30-minute steady window for throughput. For p99 stability we'll stitch together several windows across days.
08:33 Maya: Is there a risk that synthetic requests hit rate limits or are flagged? We use WAF and API protections.
08:40 Lena: We'll coordinate IP allowlists for the lab runs. Also Redwood will run with a test API key and dedicated route to avoid impacting production.
08:52 Priya: Ok. Timeline — you mentioned 6 weeks. What are the phases?
09:00 Lena: Phase 0: data handoff and setup (week 0) — EmberTech provides traces and prompt sets. Phase 1: lab sweep and benchmarking (week 1) — Redwood runs warm/cold sweeps and shares initial results. Phase 2: tuning and iteration (weeks 2–3) — batching/cache/quantization tweaks. Phase 3: pilot traffic handoff and monitoring (weeks 4–5). Phase 4: review and acceptance (week 6).
09:31 Rajesh: Sounds good. Any fallbacks if targets aren't met?
09:36 Samir: Yes — fallback ladder: 1) increase batch windows for cost tradeoff, 2) move to a narrower model variant with faster kernels, 3) provision additional dedicated capacity temporarily, 4) degrade to model with lower generation length cap for critical routes. We'll document rollback steps.
09:58 Priya: We want to avoid changing model outputs during normal business hours. Any changes will be scheduled in a maintenance window.
10:06 Lena: Noted.
10:10 Rajesh: Let's lock down concrete SLO numbers to put in the SOW.
10:14 Samir: Proposed SLOs by traffic bucket:
 - Short (<=32 tokens): TTFT p95 <= 140ms, TTFT p99 <= 320ms, TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token
 - Medium (33–128): TTFT p95 <= 180ms, TTFT p99 <= 420ms, TPOT p95 <= 22–30ms/token depending on batching
 - Long (>128): TTFT p95 <= 300ms, TTFT p99 <= 700ms, TPOT p95 <= 35–50ms/token
10:55 Rajesh: Those are reasonable. For billing we'll also want per-route SLOs; some routes are high-value and need Tier A.
11:07 Lena: We'll include route-level SLO mapping and an acceptance matrix in the sheet.
11:13 Priya: Measurement specifics — what sample size for p99 in the long bucket? Long responses are rarer.
11:20 Samir: We will combine synthetic augmentation for the long bucket to reach at least 5k samples — but we'll flag synthetic samples separately. Acceptance will require a mix: min 1k real samples + 4k synthetic to reach confidence.
11:40 Rajesh: Makes sense. Also want to track cold-start percentiles when autoscaling triggers new instances.
11:47 Ava: We'll instrument instance spin-up times and model load time as separate metrics. Track cold-start p95 and p99.
11:57 Maya: For compliance, store only aggregated latency metrics in our systems. Raw traces will be encrypted and ephemeral.
12:04 Lena: We'll send the retention policy and KMS options.
12:09 Tom: One more budget note: please provide cost delta for hitting Tier A vs Tier B in monthly terms.
12:17 Lena: Will do.
12:21 Rajesh: Anything else on runbook?
12:24 Samir: We'll prepare a runbook covering: who to call for incidents, how to revert model variants, how to toggle batch/quantization profiles, and automated alerts for SLO degradation (e.g., p95 jump >20% over baseline).
12:40 Priya: Alerts need to flow into our PagerDuty channel. We'll share integration details.
12:46 Lena: Ok. Final check — acceptance criteria recap: pass both latency (TTFT p95/p99 targets per bucket) and throughput (TPOT p95) and no significant model quality regression on the golden prompts. Also agree minimal sample counts per bucket.
13:05 Rajesh: We agree.
13:10 Lena: Great. I'll follow up with the benchmark sheet and SOW draft. Any objections?
13:18 Priya: None.
13:20 Tom: No.
13:23 Lena: Thanks everyone, we'll action items and reconvene after the lab sweep.
